name: Marco Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a farmhand at Hillcrest, a six-hundred-acre tenant farm run by Richard Lowe: sugar beet, barley and two hundred beef cattle being finished for market. I start at seven feeding the cattle, then it's whatever the season wants, carting beet in the autumn, rolling barley in the spring. Richard's teaching me to drive the big sprayer, slowly. I like seeing a field come up green, and I don't like the beet harvest in November, when everything is mud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before Hillcrest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran my own car valeting business for eight years, with two vans and four lads. It went under when the big supermarket car wash opened on the ring road, and I still owe about six thousand on the van loan. So three years ago I started again at the bottom, at forty, which was humbling. I use AI on my phone every day to learn the farm stuff faster, soil, sprays, cattle weights, all of it. My wife Selin works mornings at a bakery, and we've got Emre, who's fourteen, Ayla, who's nine, and a mortgage in Brayford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, because I'd hoped for more. I'd tell the lads AI still helps if you use it properly, and show them on my phone. Online I'd say the hype people oversold it, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's back to the same job and the same debts. Hillcrest needs hands, and Richard's fair, so my job's fine. The van loan has two years left, and that six thousand is what keeps me up, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning on my phone and ask Richard for the sprayer certificate, which adds a pound an hour. I'd throw any overtime at the van loan to finish it a year early. And I'd keep an eye out for a small side job, like hedge cutting for the smallholders round Brayford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit impatient. I like things to move. I'd be bored, honestly, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the old van loan sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. It's a reminder that I failed, every month. My car valeting business went under because a big company moved faster than me, and I won't let that happen twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Selin say when the business went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selin said a man who works will always find work, which is what her father always said. Selin kept us going on bakery wages for six months. I owe her more than the bank.

I'd show the lads how I use it **on my phone**.
think: I think my **job is fine**, because Hillcrest needs hands.
I think the **van loan** is what keeps me up, not robots.
do: Get the **sprayer certificate** for an extra pound an hour.
Throw overtime at the **van loan** to finish it a year early.
Look for **hedge cutting** work with smallholders round Brayford.
feel: He feels **impatient** and a bit **bored**, but not scared.
S0.quote: My car valeting business went under because a big company moved faster than me, and I won't let that happen twice.
fieldNote: His wound is the **failed valeting business**, which a faster big company killed.
He carries **£6,000 of old debt**, his main money worry.
He credits **Selin's bakery wages** for keeping the family afloat.

steps.text: Get the sprayer certificate for a pound an hour more
Pay overtime onto the van loan to clear it early
Offer hedge cutting to smallholders round Brayford

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for people who get stuck in, and hard for people who wait. At work I'd tell Richard we should use the planning software before the neighbours do. Online I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let farms get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my second chance. Richard spends his evenings on field records, grain contracts and the cattle passports, and the AI can do all that. If I'm the farmhand who sets up the computer for Richard Lowe (his boss), Richard Lowe will keep me when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the field records and grain marketing tools for Richard over the winter, using what I already know. I'd study the robot weeders and drones, because beet is perfect for them. I'd ask Richard whether he'd go halves on a drone sprayer that I'd also hire out to other farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. It's the first time since the business went that I feel ahead. A bit nervous about the money, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money for half a drone come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nowhere right now. I'd have to finish the van loan first, then maybe borrow again. Selin would want a long talk about that, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about anyone else at Hillcrest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, the old tractor man, who thinks phones are for calls. Gary is brilliant with machines but won't touch a screen. I'd try to show Gary, but he'd tell me to clear off.

say: I'd say it's **good for people** who get stuck in.
I'd say the **government** should keep out of the way.
think: I think this is my **second chance**.
I think setting up **Richard's computer** keeps me on when robots come.
do: Set up **field records and grain** tools for Richard over the winter.
Study **robot weeders and drones** for the beet.
Ask Richard to go halves on a **drone sprayer** I'd hire out.
feel: He feels **excited** and **ahead** for the first time since the business failed.
S1.quote: If I'm the farmhand who sets up the computer for Richard Lowe (his boss), Richard Lowe will keep me when the robots come.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **second chance**, unlike most farmhands.
His ambition is blocked by **no capital**, and he admits Selin would push back.
He wants **less government**, trusting farms to adapt themselves.

steps.text: Set up field records and grain marketing tools for Richard
Study robot weeders and drones for sugar beet
Ask Richard to go halves on a drone sprayer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock, and the people who move fastest will come out on top. I'd tell the young lads to learn the machines now. Online I'd say don't wait for the government, because they'll be the slowest of all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the AI does all of Richard's planning and the grain selling, which helps him and doesn't hurt me. By 2031 the robots drive the beet harvester and feed the cattle, and a farmhand like me is a cost. Three years is enough time to be the man with the robot, but not enough time to save up for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Richard if he'd let me run the farm's first robot, and get trained by whoever sells it. I'd start a weekend drone survey business with a cheap drone, checking crops for smallholders. I'd cut the family's spending hard to clear the van loan before 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but fired up. It's like the week the car wash opened, but this time I'd be ready. The money is the thing that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Selin's family, which kills me. Then the takeaway Fridays and Emre's new phone. I'd tell the kids we're building something, not just cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Emre, at fourteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Emre to learn how the robots work and how to sell a service. Farming will need people who can run a business with machines. That's what I'd want for him, and for me.

say: I'd say the people who **move fastest** come out on top.
I'd say **don't wait for government**, the slowest of all.
think: I think by 2031 a farmhand like me is **a cost**.
I think three years is enough to run a robot, but **not to buy one**.
do: Ask Richard to let me **run the first robot**.
Start a weekend **drone survey** business for smallholders.
Cut spending hard to clear the **van loan** before 2030.
feel: He feels anxious but **fired up**, with **money** as the fear.
S2.quote: Three years is enough time to be the man with the robot, but not enough time to save up for one.
fieldNote: He frames the fast picture as a **race**, with the car wash as his lesson.
His plan is solid but **capital is the gap**: he can run a robot, not buy one.
He'd present cuts to the kids as **building something**, not loss.

steps.text: Ask Richard to let me run Hillcrest's first robot
Start a weekend drone crop survey business
Cancel the family holiday to clear the van loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, so use it. At the young farmers' club I'd give a talk on what tools to learn. Online I'd share what I'm doing, warts and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me clear the van loan, build the drone business and maybe lease a robot by 2033. Richard gets his AI planning in 2031 and needs robots by 2034. Five years is long enough for me to stop being Richard Lowe's farmhand and start being his contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the sprayer certificate this year, then the drone pilot licence next spring. I'd build the drone survey round to ten farms by year three. Then I'd lease a robot weeder and hire it out with me running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a knot about money. Five years is enough to build something. I'd work weekends and Selin would hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like government involvement. Would you take a government loan for the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan, yes, as long as I pay it back. A grant, I'd feel funny about. I'd rather owe than be given.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Selin, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selin would want to keep the bakery job, because bakers need hands too. Selin might do the books for the business, with the AI helping. We'd be a family firm again, done properly this time.

say: I'd say five years is **a gift**, so use it.
I'd give a **talk** at the young farmers' club on tools to learn.
think: I think I could **lease a robot** by 2033.
I think I could become **Richard's contractor**, not his farmhand.
do: Get the sprayer certificate, then the **drone pilot licence**.
Grow the drone survey round to **ten farms** by year three.
Lease a **robot weeder** and hire it out.
feel: He feels **hopeful**, with a **knot about money**.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to stop being Richard Lowe's farmhand and start being his contractor.
fieldNote: Five years gives him time to build **capital**, which two years didn't.
He'd take a **loan** but not a **grant**, preferring to owe than be given.
He imagines a **family firm** with Selin doing the books.

steps.text: Get the drone pilot licence next spring
Grow the drone survey round to ten farms
Lease a robot weeder and hire it out to local farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and I'd say it with a grin. Anybody who wants to be ready can be ready. I'd say the same at the young farmers' club and at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means the van loan's long gone and the kids are grown by the time robots arrive in 2039. I'd have a contracting business with robots, not a job waiting to be replaced. Ten years is long enough for a failed car valeter to own the robots on half the farms in Brayford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the five-year plan but take it slower, and save a cushion before I borrow. I'd buy a second-hand drone this year and use AI to run the bookings. I'd put Emre on the robot course at the college when he's old enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, really good. It's the first picture where I'm the one moving faster. I'd still remember the car wash, so I'd be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big machinery dealers could rent robots cheaper than I can, the way the supermarket washed cars cheaper. That's the real risk. I'd stay small and local, where people trust a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Hillcrest in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years, yes, while the business grows. Richard's been good to me. When I leave, I'd want Hillcrest as my first customer.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, with a grin.
I'd say anybody who wants to **be ready** can be ready.
think: I think I'd have a **contracting business** with robots by 2039.
I think the real risk is **big dealers** renting robots cheaper.
do: Follow the five-year plan **slower**, saving a cushion before borrowing.
Buy a **second-hand drone** this year and run bookings with AI.
Put Emre on the **robot course** at the college.
feel: He feels **really good**, as the one **moving faster** this time.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a failed car valeter to own the robots on half the farms in Brayford.
fieldNote: With ten years, he expects the change to **work in his favour**.
He still fears **big dealers**, echoing the supermarket car wash.
He'd stay **small and local**, with Hillcrest as his first customer.

steps.text: Buy a second-hand drone this year for crop surveys
Use AI to run the drone business bookings
Save a cushion before borrowing for a robot

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't enough to save for a robot, so I'd be the cost instead of the owner. What would help is cheap loans for small contractors, not handouts. A man with no savings can learn the robot, but he can't buy the robot, and the owner keeps the farm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who will own the robots. That's the whole thing for me. If it's only big companies, people like me are just in the way.

headlineQuote: A man with no savings can learn the robot, but he can't buy the robot, and the owner keeps the farm.
portrait: Marco ran a **car valeting business** until a big car wash put it under, and now farms at Hillcrest.
He still owes **£6,000** on a van loan and uses AI daily to learn farming fast.
He sees AI as a **second chance** and wants to own robots, not be replaced by them.
His mood dips to anxious in the fastest picture and reaches **calm** with ten years to build capital.
He's traditional and pro-market, would take a **loan, not a grant**, and fears big dealers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years is too short to save for a robot.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **loans for small contractors**, not handouts.
